title: I've been building an automated Linux GPU provisioning system — could this approach be useful for game development?
author: Double_Grand_3799
selftext:
I've been working on an open-source side project called No Land that automates turning rented GPU machines into fully configured Linux gaming PCs.

The original goal was cloud gaming, but some of the infrastructure challenges have made me curious about other possible uses.

The app connects to rented machines on [Vast.ai](http://Vast.ai) over SSH and automatically prepares the environment.

It handles NVIDIA drivers, GPU persistence, Sunshine/NVENC, audio, networking, WireGuard tunnels, storage, and remote access.

The provisioning system also includes parallel execution, precompiled helper agents, adaptive polling, checksums, and recovery from interrupted operations.

One of the things I've focused on is persistent storage across instances, so files don't necessarily disappear when you destroy one rented machine and start another.

For the gaming use case, I've managed to run Cyberpunk 2077 at 3K Ultra, 60 FPS, with around 62 ms latency over a 4,000+ km connection between Vancouver and Quebec.

That got me thinking about whether similar infrastructure could be useful for remote graphics testing or giving developers temporary access to more powerful hardware.

The project wasn't originally designed as a game-development tool, so I haven't validated those workflows yet.

It's open source:

[https://github.com/FelipeBarrosCode/no\_land](https://github.com/FelipeBarrosCode/no_land)

Gameplay demo:

[https://no-land.net/](https://no-land.net/)

I'd be interested in learning how developers currently handle temporary GPU environments for testing, especially when they don't have powerful local hardware.
